entry.title: Mark Zuckerberg criticizes closed AI competitors as Meta shifts back to open AI models
entry.summary: Mark Zuckerberg has publicly criticized rival AI companies for their closed approaches while announcing Meta's return to developing open AI models. This marks a strategic shift for Meta as it emphasizes openness in AI development compared to competitors who maintain proprietary systems. The move reflects Meta's intent to differentiate itself in the AI landscape by promoting transparency and collaboration through open models.

entry.title: Cactus Compute launches Needle2, a 14MB agentic LLM designed for low-cost devices like phones, wearables, smart home gadgets, and robots [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Cactus Compute has introduced Needle2, a 14MB agentic large language model (LLM) optimized for devices costing under $200, including budget phones, wearables, smart home devices, and small robots. Needle2 operates without GPUs or NPUs, using a 45 million parameter model tailored for function call mapping rather than open-ended chat, enabling efficient on-device AI with low latency and privacy. The model employs lossless 2-bit quantization trained end-to-end, a co-designed inference engine in a single C++ binary compatible across hardware from Cortex-M to x86, and supports fine-tuning on local machines. Needle2 is production-ready and already deployed in Pebble's Index 01 app to process voice commands offline, ensuring reliable performance without network dependency.

entry.title: Meta releases Muse Glimmer, a 30B-parameter open-source model optimized for always-on local AI agent workflows on consumer hardware [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Meta Superintelligence Labs has introduced Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter AI model designed to run locally on devices like Macs or PCs with a single consumer GPU. The model supports always-on agent workflows including local coding, function calling, and evaluation tasks, and is released under an Apache 2.0 license with open weights available on Hugging Face. Muse Glimmer was trained using a novel distillation process from a larger teacher model and optimized for local deployment with quantization and inference improvements. It supports multimodal inputs, multi-step reasoning, failure recovery, and multilingual capabilities across more than 100 languages. The model performs strongly on benchmarks for autonomous agent behavior and is compatible with existing developer tools and agent orchestration frameworks.

entry.title: Analysis: Humanising large language model outputs during processing reduces information fidelity and obscures failures, argues blog post [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent blog post argues that instructing AI agents to produce human-friendly outputs as part of their core processing leads to lossy compression and loss of critical information. The author highlights that while human-readable summaries are appealing, they can hide important details such as errors, conflicting evidence, or test failures that are better preserved in raw, machine-readable formats. The post suggests that AI systems should maintain high-fidelity, precise internal representations and only convert outputs into simplified or humanized forms at the final stage for user consumption. This approach contrasts with current trends where humanisation instructions are embedded early in the AI's workflow, potentially reducing transparency and diagnostic value. The author acknowledges the value of accessibility and personalization but recommends these be applied as rendering layers rather than core operational constraints.

entry.title: Researchers find linear probes detect corrupted context in language models but fail to reliably predict final answer errors across multiple model families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study reveals that while linear probes can identify corrupted inputs in language models with near-perfect accuracy, this ability does not translate into reliable predictions of whether the model's final answers are correct. The research shows that confidence measures collapse into indistinguishable error rates and that probe persistence does not differentiate between correct and incorrect outcomes, a pattern consistent across various reasoning models. Probe-based interventions vary in effectiveness depending on the model and error type, with some strategies like branch-and-pick showing promise on specific models such as Llama-3.1-8B, while others may disrupt correct outputs as often as they fix errors. The findings suggest that probe-based monitoring should complement verbalized confidence and be tailored to specific deployment contexts rather than relying on a single universal approach.

entry.title: Research proposes an Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework for hospital information systems to enable governed ecosystems of autonomous agents across workflows [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: A new research paper introduces a compliance-focused Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework designed for Hospital Information Management Systems (HIMS) to move beyond isolated AI chatbots. The framework supports critical hospital workflows such as triage, documentation, scheduling, and revenue management by coordinating autonomous and semi-autonomous agents within a governed ecosystem. The framework includes a taxonomy of agent roles, a risk-stratification model with governance checkpoints, and a unified orchestration runtime compatible with major EHR systems like Epic, Cerner, and MEDITECH. It integrates technologies such as vLLM-based inference, confidential computing, and policy-as-code controls aligned with regulations including HIPAA, GDPR, and the EU AI Act. The approach aims to reduce documentation time, ease integration, improve governance and auditability, and provide hospitals with a blueprint for sustainable clinical, operational, and financial returns on AI investments.

entry.title: GRACE introduces an LLM-grounded framework for scalable mixed-data clustering, combining semantic representations with dataset statistics to improve accuracy and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: GRACE is a new framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to create unified semantic metric spaces for clustering mixed tabular data containing both numerical and categorical values. It addresses the challenge of bridging heterogeneous data types by grounding semantic acquisition at the attribute-value level through multi-perspective LLM queries, enabling one-shot extraction of general-purpose semantic embeddings without iterative LLM calls. GRACE also cross-validates these external semantic representations with internal dataset statistics to align with specific cluster structures, achieving scalability comparable to traditional methods while outperforming 11 existing clustering approaches in accuracy and interpretability. The source code for GRACE is publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers analyze quantization degradation in large language models using signal-to-noise ratio, revealing variability across bit-widths, tasks, methods, and model scales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers systematically study weight-only post-training quantization in large language models, finding that performance degradation varies significantly with bit-width, quantization method, model scale, and downstream tasks. They observe that 4-bit quantization generally preserves performance, 2-bit causes broad degradation, and 3-bit results vary depending on multiple factors. The study uses signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to measure how quantization errors affect full-precision representations, identifying two key processes: error introduction within modules and error accumulation across layers. They find that error magnitude, task-specific signal strength, and alignment of quantization error with task activations influence degradation, while larger models tend to experience weaker error amplification across layers. These findings clarify how quantization errors impact model performance and vary with different conditions.

entry.title: HoloAegis introduces a minimally parametric topological inference framework for zero-shot LLM safety guardrails using frozen semantic representations and geometric reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: HoloAegis presents a new approach to large language model (LLM) safety by using geometric reasoning over frozen semantic representations instead of fine-tuning or generative judges, which can distort models or incur high inference costs. The framework relies on a fixed encoder mapping text to a unit sphere and uses a System Topology Anchor Bank with Gibbs-Boltzmann Free Energy computations to evaluate safety, along with Dual Time-Scale Exponential Moving Averages to detect semantic drift. The method is minimally parametric, requiring only two fixed parameters after construction, and is supported by a Topological Boundary Stability Conjecture that sparse anchor centroids stabilize decision boundaries better than full vector space methods. Evaluated on eight benchmarks, HoloAegis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with sub-millisecond latency, no cold-start data, and effective cross-lingual transfer, including strong performance on Chinese datasets.

entry.title: Researchers apply Marchenko-Pastur random matrix theory to transformer attention weights, identifying spectral outliers that encode dominant learned structure across 11 pre-trained models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers used Marchenko-Pastur random matrix theory to analyze pre-trained transformer attention weights, separating projection matrices into random-like bulk and spectral outliers. They found that zeroing out these outliers in the Mistral-7B model significantly degrades performance on benchmarks like HellaSwag, MMLU, and PIQA, while removing bulk singular values causes smaller effects. Across 11 transformers, they observed consistent patterns including the concentration of outliers in Q projections and structured band patterns in certain projections. The study suggests these findings could guide parameter-efficient fine-tuning and structured pruning strategies for transformers.

entry.title: Researchers propose carbon-aware fine-tuning to optimize Large Language Model inference accuracy and emissions across multiple architectures and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers investigate whether integrating a calibrated, differentiable energy surrogate into the fine-tuning objective of Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve task accuracy improvements at zero or near-zero carbon cost during inference. They develop a joint loss mechanism incorporating a per-model carbon-emission parameter based on hardware energy profiling and fine-tune three distinct LLM families-Gemma-2 2B, Llama-3.1 8B, and Qwen-2.5 14B-evaluating performance and CO2 emissions on tasks in abstract algebra, philosophy, and formal logic. The study finds that the carbon term can act as either harmful interference or beneficial regularization depending on the task, suggesting that calibrated carbon-aware fine-tuning can serve as a lightweight, task-dependent regularizer to balance performance and emissions. This ongoing work aims to release its codebase soon.

entry.title: Researchers present Guardian Crawler, a retrieval-first testbed combining BM25 and LLM augmentation for knowledge discovery on noisy synthetic web data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Guardian Crawler is a reproducible testbed designed for controlled experiments in knowledge discovery and evidence-grounded summarization over synthetic web-like corpora with noisy data. It integrates BM25 retrieval with risk-aware, embedding-augmented, and hybrid reranking, followed by constrained retrieval-augmented generation that includes explicit document citations. Experiments on a synthetic corpus of 900 documents and 10 queries showed improved retrieval scores, with risk-based reranking achieving P@10 of 1.00 and NDCG@10 of 0.94 compared to BM25's 0.94 and 0.81 respectively. An automated LLM judge classified most generated summaries as supported or partially supported, demonstrating the system's feasibility as a controlled testbed. However, the results do not establish statistical superiority, human-validated faithfulness, or applicability to live web investigative environments.

entry.title: Researchers analyze overconfidence in large language models under clinical uncertainty, revealing misaligned confidence and increased unsafe errors in medical question answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted a systematic analysis of large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering under conditions of clinical uncertainty, using the MedMCQA dataset with two uncertainty settings: linguistic ambiguity and deliberate removal of correct answers. They found that while model accuracy decreases with uncertainty, model confidence does not align with accuracy, leading to a rise in confidently incorrect answers that could mislead clinical decisions. The study also observed variability among models in their ability to abstain when correct answers are unavailable, with some models producing high-confidence hallucinated responses. These findings highlight significant limitations in the reliability of current LLMs and underscore the need for uncertainty-aware evaluation before deploying these models in clinical workflows.

entry.title: MoRSE introduces a task-oriented multi-agent system with role-subtask specialization and parameter adaptation using a mixture of experts and hierarchical policy optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: MoRSE presents a multi-agent system that enhances large language model performance on complex, long-horizon tasks by assigning agents specific roles and subtasks within a dependency-aware task graph and enabling parameter-level specialization through a mixture of role-subtask experts. The system uses a prototype-based semantic router and hierarchical group-relative policy optimization to co-optimize experts and routing decisions, improving both whole-task and step-wise performance on code-generation benchmarks across multiple model backbones. These improvements generalize across unseen task categories and domains, demonstrating the effectiveness of explicit task decomposition and specialized parameter adaptation in multi-agent collaboration.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Perturbed Parameter Policy Optimization (3PO) for parameter-space exploration in reinforcement learning of LLMs, improving performance on math and code tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a new family of methods called Perturbed Parameter Policy Optimization (3PO) that explore parameter space by sampling different policies from a posterior, aiming to improve reinforcement learning for large language models (LLMs). This approach contrasts with traditional action-space exploration methods and seeks to enhance downstream task performance by generating more diverse rollouts. Experiments on OLMo-3-1025-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B models across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks demonstrate that 3PO consistently outperforms standard GRPO methods at similar computational costs. The use of multiple parameter samples reduces the occurrence of zero-advantage groups and malformed or incorrect rollouts during training compared to action-space baselines, suggesting that parameter-space exploration can be a valuable tool in LLM reinforcement learning.

entry.title: Researchers introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework using sparse autoencoders to identify and control features in multimodal large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed MMDiff, a framework that trains multimodal sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to discover and control internal features responsible for multimodal behaviors in large language models. MMDiff enables feature isolation by comparing base language models with their multimodal counterparts, detects task-specific causal features, and allows feature-level control by removing or steering these features. The team trained multimodal SAEs on three model families-LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5-and evaluated them on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and optical character recognition (OCR). Removing identified features degraded spatial and OCR task performance by 12% and 17% respectively, and reduced multimodal safety attack success by 24%, without affecting visual question answering. Steering these features improved spatial and OCR accuracy by 3.6% and 1.8% over baseline methods. These results demonstrate that multimodal SAEs can serve as tools not only for interpretability but also for auditing, steering, and controlling multimodal large language model behaviors to enhance safety and capability.

entry.title: Researchers identify information-theoretic limits in decoder-only attention causing extended reasoning failures on deterministic state-tracking tasks, proposing tool delegation to improve accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present evidence that extended chain-of-thought reasoning degrades performance on deterministic state-tracking tasks due to information-theoretic limits in decoder-only attention capacity rather than preference biases. They introduce an Attention Bottleneck analysis, a context-dependent error model, a State-Space Jaccard metric for state drift, and define a Deterministic Horizon marking when unaided accuracy falls below 50%. Across twelve models and eight task domains, tool-integrated reasoning achieves 76-94% accuracy compared to 17-42% for neural chain-of-thought methods. Fine-tuning on optimal-length traces yields minimal improvement, indicating an architectural ceiling.

entry.title: Researchers release Transformer Explainer, an interactive tool for learning Transformer models with live GPT-2 experiments and layered visual explanations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Transformer Explainer, an interactive visualization tool designed to help non-experts understand Transformer architectures that power large language models. The tool features an overview of data flow, on-demand mathematical explanations, and runs a live GPT-2 model in the browser, allowing users to experiment with inputs and hyperparameters without setup. A user study with 90 participants showed significant improvements in understanding and engagement, and the tool has attracted over 490,000 users.

entry.title: Researchers introduce WebChoreArena to evaluate web browsing agents on 532 complex, tedious tasks requiring massive memory, calculation, and long-term memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed WebChoreArena, an extension of the WebArena benchmark, to assess the capabilities of web browsing agents powered by large language models (LLMs) on more labor-intensive and cognitively demanding web tasks. WebChoreArena includes 532 curated tasks designed to test agents' abilities in massive memory retention, precise calculation, and consistent long-term memory across multiple webpages, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks. Built on the four reproducible WebArena environments, WebChoreArena allows fair comparisons with prior work and was developed over 300+ hours. Experimental results show that while LLMs like GPT-5 demonstrate significant improvements on WebChoreArena, substantial challenges remain compared to performance on WebArena, indicating the increased difficulty of these tasks and the benchmark's suitability for measuring future advancements in web browsing agents.

entry.title: Researchers release MateInfoUB, a bilingual English-Romanian multimodal dataset to benchmark LLMs on competitive computer science tasks with code and reasoning challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed MateInfoUB, a bilingual (English-Romanian) multimodal dataset featuring multiple-choice questions from a high-level computer science competition designed to test large language models (LLMs) on both code-based and reasoning tasks. The dataset highlights differences in problem-solving approaches, with some questions better suited for paper reasoning and others for coding, and evaluates state-of-the-art LLMs' performance across these challenges. The study analyzes the impact of language choice on LLM performance and discusses ethical concerns related to educational integrity and fairness in assessments involving AI tools. To facilitate further research and practical use, the dataset will be publicly available in both languages, accompanied by an educational application aimed at Romanian students for interactive self-assessment and practice.

entry.title: Quokka framework uses large language models to synthesize loop invariants for program verification, achieving state-of-the-art performance with soundness guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Quokka is a new framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate loop invariants, a key component in program verification, addressing the challenge of automatically discovering strong invariants. Unlike previous methods that require extensive post-processing of LLM outputs, Quokka directly validates each generated invariant to prove target assertions, improving efficiency and reliability. The framework was evaluated on a benchmark derived from SV-COMP, consisting of 866 evaluation instances and 3589 training instances, across nine different LLMs from multiple model families. Results show that supervised fine-tuning and Best-of-N sampling enhance performance, with Quokka consistently outperforming prior LLM-based verification approaches. The code and data for Quokka are publicly available for further research and development.

entry.title: NeuroAda introduces bypass connections for fine-grained parameter-efficient fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art results with under 0.02% trainable parameters and up to 60% CUDA memory reduction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: NeuroAda is a new parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that balances fine-grained adaptation and memory efficiency by identifying important network connections and updating only bypass connections while keeping original parameters frozen. It outperforms existing methods on over 23 natural language tasks, using minimal trainable parameters and significantly reducing memory usage. The approach combines the precision of selective adaptation with the efficiency of addition-based methods, offering improved performance for natural language generation and understanding tasks.

entry.title: Researchers introduce semantic isotropy as a low-cost method to predict nonfactuality in long-form text generated by large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose semantic isotropy, measured as the angular dispersion of normalized text embeddings, to assess the factual consistency of long-form responses generated by large language models (LLMs). This method requires no labeled data, fine-tuning, or hyperparameter tuning and can be applied with various embedding models to provide a computationally inexpensive trustworthiness signal. The approach outperforms existing aggregate trust signals across multiple domains using only a few samples, offering a practical first-pass tool that complements detailed claim-level fact-checking in real-world LLM applications where accuracy is critical.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Length-MAX tokenizer that reduces tokens per character and speeds GPT-2 training with improved downstream task performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed the Length-MAX tokenizer, which minimizes average tokens per character to reduce token count during training and inference for language models. This tokenizer uses a length-weighted objective maximization framed as a graph partitioning problem and a greedy approximation algorithm, achieving 14-18% fewer tokens than Byte Pair Encoding across various vocabulary sizes. Training GPT-2 models of 124M, 355M, and 1.3B parameters from scratch showed 17-18.5% fewer steps to reach fixed validation loss and 12.7-13.7% lower inference latency, along with a 16% throughput gain at 124M parameters. The tokenizer also improved downstream tasks, reducing LAMBADA perplexity by 11.7% and increasing HellaSwag accuracy by 4.3%, while maintaining 99.62% vocabulary coverage and a low 0.12% out-of-vocabulary rate. The Length-MAX tokenizer is compatible with production systems and reduces embedding and KV-cache memory usage by 18% during inference, demonstrating that optimizing for average token length can enhance language model efficiency without sacrificing performance.

entry.title: Researchers propose Merlin-Arthur protocol framework to reduce hallucinations in retrieval-augmented language models by treating retrieved context as verifiable evidence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a novel framework adapting the Merlin-Arthur interactive proof system to improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in large language models (LLMs), addressing hallucinations and unsupported answers by treating retrieved context as verifiable evidence. The framework includes an evaluation, data augmentation, and training method where the generator LLM (Arthur) receives context, Merlin provides helpful evidence, and Morgana injects adversarial context, implemented with explainable AI techniques to assess influential evidence. The team proposes the Explained Information Fraction (EIF) score to separate explanation fidelity from model errors and benchmarks, normalizing mutual-information bounds in practical settings. Training with this framework across five question-answering benchmarks and four LLMs (1B to 32B parameters) reduced incorrect answers under insufficient context by up to 35 percentage points during training and 18-20 points compared to standard finetuning. The approach also improved retriever recall and enabled the model to abstain from answering when evidence was insufficient, without requiring manually annotated unanswerable examples. These results demonstrate that autonomous interactive-proof-style supervision can enable RAG systems to treat retrieved documents as reliable evidence, potentially improving the trustworthiness and accuracy of language model outputs.

entry.title: ROM framework detects and intervenes in real-time to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models, improving accuracy and cutting response length by up to 77% across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often continue unnecessary reasoning steps after reaching a correct solution, wasting computation and sometimes reversing correct answers. Researchers propose ROM, a streaming intervention framework that monitors hidden states in frozen LRMs to detect when overthinking begins and intervenes at reasoning boundaries without modifying the model or extracting intermediate answers. ROM uses a lightweight detector and Counterfactual Self-Correction to balance supervision and preserve useful self-correction before the first correct solution. ROM was tested across five model backbones from three families and five reasoning benchmarks, outperforming ten recent baselines by achieving the highest accuracy in 19 of 25 model-benchmark settings. It reduces response length by 28-77% (mean 45%) compared to standard decoding and lowers end-to-end latency by 46.5% with minimal per-token overhead. The supervision trained on MATH500 transfers zero-shot across different scales, model families, and task domains. The code for ROM is publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers propose SPA, a prompt-engineered augmentation method that generates large-scale synthetic data for knowledge injection, outperforming existing baselines in specialized domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce SPA (Scaling Prompt-engineered Augmentation), a method that uses a small set of carefully designed prompts to create large-scale synthetic data for injecting knowledge into large language models (LLMs). SPA outperforms several strong baselines and addresses limitations found in prior approaches such as diversity collapse in reinforcement learning-based methods and diminishing advantages of multi-stage prompting after prompt tuning. The study suggests that careful prompt design combined with straightforward large-scale augmentation is an effective strategy for knowledge injection in data-scarce domains, and the researchers have made their code publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers study trade-offs between pretraining and retrieval in language models up to 3B parameters across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers systematically analyze how retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) interacts with pretraining in language models ranging from 30 million to 3 billion parameters, trained on up to 100 billion tokens. They vary pretraining data scale, retrieval store size, and data source across reasoning, scientific question answering, and open-domain QA tasks to understand performance impacts. The study finds that retrieval benefits depend on model size and pretraining exposure, with most gains achieved early using one retrieval token per model parameter. Smaller models improve more in perplexity, while larger, well-pretrained models gain more in accuracy. Retrieval from previously seen data retains most benefits, suggesting that retrieval complements parametric learning depending on task, model regime, metric, datastore size, and novelty of information. This supports designing language models with explicit separation between internalized knowledge and external retrieval access.

entry.title: Researchers introduce TraceSafe-Bench to evaluate safety guardrails in multi-step LLM tool-use trajectories, revealing structural data competence as key to efficacy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed TraceSafe-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark to assess safety guardrails during multi-step tool-use trajectories in large language models (LLMs). The benchmark covers 12 risk categories including security threats and operational failures, with over 1,000 execution instances. Evaluations of 13 LLM-based guard models and 7 specialized guardrails identified that guardrail effectiveness depends more on structural data handling than semantic safety alignment, model size does not predict detection accuracy, and detection performance varies with trajectory length, declining in very long contexts due to over-refusal. The study highlights that general-purpose LLMs outperform specialized safety guardrails and that performance correlates strongly with structured-to-text processing benchmarks rather than traditional jailbreak robustness. These findings suggest that improving structural data competence is crucial for enhancing mid-trajectory safety in autonomous LLM agents, with implications for future development of more reliable AI safety mechanisms.

entry.title: Researchers propose Path-Lock Expert architecture to separate reasoning modes in hybrid-thinking language models, reducing reasoning leakage and improving accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Path-Lock Expert (PLE), an architecture-level modification for hybrid-thinking language models that replaces the single MLP in each decoder layer with two mode-specific experts for /think and /no_think modes. This design uses a deterministic control-token router to select one expert path per sequence, maintaining per-token computation patterns and enabling mode-pure updates during fine-tuning. PLE demonstrates stronger mode separation, reducing reasoning leakage and improving /no_think accuracy while preserving /think performance across math and science reasoning benchmarks. For example, on the Qwen3-4B model tested on AIME24, PLE reduced reflective tokens by 17 times and output length by half, increasing /no_think accuracy from 35.33% to 44.67% without degrading /think-mode accuracy. These results suggest that architectural separation of feed-forward pathways is an effective solution for controllable hybrid thinking in language models.

entry.title: Researchers propose DeltaPrompts, a synthetic dataset to improve multimodal distillation by targeting high-divergence prompts and overcoming zero-delta inefficiencies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers identify that up to 69% of prompts in standard vision-language model distillation datasets yield no learning signal due to identical teacher and student answer distributions, limiting model improvement. They introduce DeltaPrompts, a dataset of 200,000 synthetic, high-divergence reasoning problems designed to expose capability gaps between teacher and student models and enhance distillation effectiveness. DeltaPrompts is generated through a staged synthesis pipeline that repurposes existing datasets and targets student failure modes. Evaluations across on-policy distillation, transfer to new model families, and off-policy fine-tuning show up to 15% relative improvement over optimized reasoning models on benchmarks involving chart, document, and perception-centric reasoning tasks.

entry.title: Researchers find consistency training improves decodability of verifier information from language model rationales but does not ensure faithful explanations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose verifier-coupled reasoning, a framework that integrates inline claims into language model rationales and trains an auxiliary consistency head to predict outputs from programmatic verifiers. Their study reveals a gap between decodability and faithfulness: while consistency training makes verifier information decodable from rationale representations, it does not guarantee that generated explanations faithfully represent the model's internal reasoning. Experiments across formal theorem proving (LeanCheck), a Go engine (KataGo), and code settings show high accuracy in encoding verifier information, but generated explanations often describe unrelated algorithms despite fluent prose and correct structured claims. Additional analyses using synthetic activation patching and evidence pooling confirm that consistency losses shape representations effectively but are insufficient for ensuring faithful reasoning. These findings highlight the limitations of current consistency training approaches as diagnostics and representation tools in language model explanation fidelity.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Epi2Diff framework using LLM reasoning traces to predict human item difficulty with improved accuracy and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Epi2Diff, a framework that maps large language model (LLM) reasoning traces into cognitive episodes to predict human item difficulty in educational assessments. This approach models difficulty based on problem-solving effort and state transitions rather than just item text, offering a more interpretable and process-oriented prediction method. Experiments on four real-world datasets show Epi2Diff outperforms existing baselines, including fine-tuned language models and in-context learning, with an 8.1% average relative gain on SAT-derived benchmarks. Epi2Diff groups reasoning trace segments into functional problem-solving states, extracting dynamic features that reflect reasoning scale and effort allocation. Analysis reveals that harder items induce more iterative and implementation-focused cognitive episodes rather than simply longer responses. These findings suggest that cognitive episodes derived from LLM reasoning traces provide a scalable and interpretable representation for assessing item difficulty, potentially enhancing fairness and effectiveness in educational measurement.

entry.title: Researchers propose UI-MOPD framework using multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train unified GUI agents across desktop and mobile platforms, improving task success rates on OSWorld and MobileWorld [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce UI-MOPD, a framework that applies multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train a shared GUI agent capable of cross-platform interaction on desktop and mobile devices. They created Uni-GUI, a dataset with nearly 10,000 executable cross-platform interaction trajectories, to support this training approach. UI-MOPD dynamically routes student rollouts to platform-specific teachers, preserving distinct interaction conventions while integrating complementary expertise. UI-MOPD achieves task success rates of 38.2% on OSWorld and 12.0% on MobileWorld, outperforming other integration strategies while maintaining general GUI grounding. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-teacher on-policy distillation for building unified multi-platform GUI agents capable of handling diverse interaction semantics and conventions.

entry.title: Researchers analyze how pretraining choices affect reinforcement learning improvements in large language models using chess and math testbeds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied the interaction between pretraining and reinforcement learning (RL) in large language models (LLMs) by using chess as a controlled environment. They pretrained models of varying sizes on human chess games, fine-tuned them on synthetic reasoning traces, and applied RL on chess puzzles with verifiable rewards to understand how pretraining influences RL returns and model behavior. The study found that post-RL performance correlates with pretraining loss and that RL reward improvements scale linearly with pretraining tokens. RL amplifies correct moves preferred by supervised fine-tuning on easy puzzles and reveals new correct moves on harder puzzles. These findings were also observed in a 1B-parameter model trained on math-domain text, suggesting the results generalize beyond chess. The work provides a quantitative framework for understanding reasoning across the full pretraining-to-post-training pipeline in LLMs.

entry.title: OpenAI sends letter to Texas Governor Abbott outlining commitment to responsible AI infrastructure development in Texas [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has sent a letter to Texas Governor Greg Abbott expressing its commitment to developing responsible AI infrastructure in the state. The company aims to collaborate with state and local leaders, utilities, and communities to ensure AI infrastructure benefits Texans effectively. The letter emphasizes OpenAI's intention to work closely with various stakeholders in Texas to promote responsible AI deployment and infrastructure management, highlighting the importance of delivering meaningful advantages to the local population.

entry.title: Analysis suggests dynamic languages may be more token-efficient than static ones for coding agents, but results vary with problem complexity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A widely cited analysis indicates that dynamic programming languages tend to use fewer tokens than static languages like Rust, Go, and C++, potentially making them more efficient for coding AI agents. The study highlights that some concise dynamic languages, such as J and Clojure, can require significantly fewer tokens, but these findings are primarily based on trivial problems that may not generalize to more complex tasks. Further evaluation reveals that initial conclusions about token efficiency may not hold for larger or more complex problems, and some test results were affected by execution errors and test design flaws. The analysis emphasizes the need for careful benchmarking and suggests that the apparent advantages of dynamic languages in token efficiency could diminish as problem difficulty increases.

entry.title: Researchers propose an active inference model incorporating valence and arousal to simulate human driving emotions in continuous state scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study introduces an enhanced active inference model for human driving that integrates affective states, specifically valence and arousal, into decision-making processes. This model extends previous approaches by handling continuous states and conditioning emotional estimates on predicted future outcomes. Evaluations in interactive driving scenarios show that the model's emotion signals correspond to affective patterns observed in similar real-world situations, suggesting improved realism in modeling driver behavior.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Data-Centric Parallel to speed up training of variable-length sequences by dynamically adjusting runtime settings, achieving up to 2.88× speedup on 32 H200 GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A new method called Data-Centric Parallel (DCP) has been developed to improve the efficiency of training deep learning models on variable-length sequences. DCP dynamically adjusts runtime parameters such as parallel size, gradient accumulation, and recomputation based on the sequence length of each batch, addressing the trade-off between efficiency and complexity found in existing approaches. Experiments demonstrate that DCP can achieve up to a 2.88 times speedup using 32 H200 GPUs. The method is designed for easy integration into any model with minimal code changes, potentially serving as a robust baseline for future distributed training advancements.

entry.title: Researchers introduce NL2SHACL-Bench to evaluate natural language to SHACL translation, testing four large language models on semantic accuracy of generated constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite designed to assess the translation of natural language requirements into SHACL shapes used for validating RDF knowledge graphs. The benchmark addresses challenges in evaluating generated SHACL shapes beyond string comparison, as semantically equivalent shapes may differ in structure and serialization. Using this benchmark, four state-of-the-art large language models were tested, showing they can produce syntactically valid SHACL but struggle with accurately capturing complex semantic constraints. NL2SHACL-Bench aims to support progress in natural language to SHACL translation technologies by providing a meaningful evaluation framework.

entry.title: Researchers propose a cooperative game framework for dynamic coalition formation and communication pricing in multi-agent AI systems using large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: The paper introduces a framework that models agent selection and communication in multi-agent AI systems as a cooperative game balancing utility and costs. It proposes a marginal-value activation rule and a greedy routing strategy to efficiently form coalitions and manage communication links, leveraging concepts like Shapley values and submodular maximization to provide theoretical performance guarantees in specific cases. Synthetic experiments show that the greedy routing achieves near-optimal utility while activating fewer agents compared to full broadcast, demonstrating robustness under various conditions. The work distinguishes itself from existing methods such as Shapley pricing and communication-graph pruning and suggests future evaluation on real multi-agent large language model benchmarks.

entry.title: Researchers develop an AI Scientist system with immutable experiment cards and a preference oracle to study quadruped robot navigation generalization without hypothesis drift [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have created an AI Scientist framework to study generalization in quadruped robot navigation policies within simulation. The system enhances the autoresearch paradigm by using immutable experiment cards to prevent retrospective hypothesis changes, specialized subagents with defined roles, and a preference oracle named kkanbu that encodes user research preferences as a typed knowledge graph. This setup aims to maintain research integrity and guide exploration based on user preferences. The team ran parallel research loops with and without the preference oracle across eleven research streams. Both approaches falsified about three quarters of their hypotheses without drifting, though the oracle influenced research direction by exploring test-time adaptation, generating successful designs, and transferring insights across streams. While the oracle did not improve overall performance scores, it shaped the focus of the research rather than the outcomes.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Controlled Memory Interference framework to analyze how long-term memory evolves in continual LLM agents, revealing interference effects that hinder updates without improving stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new framework called Controlled Memory Interference (CMI) has been developed to study how long-term memory in AI agents changes when different memories interact. The research shows that memory evolution involves not only accumulating information but also how new experiences can reinforce, revise, or interfere with existing memories, affecting update plasticity and stability. The study finds that specific types of interference can block memory updates or disrupt their use, with different retrieval methods exhibiting distinct interference patterns. CMI also supports developing memory learning approaches that better distinguish valid updates from interference, improving the reliability of continual memory systems in AI agents.

entry.title: Researchers propose Multilayer Combinatorial Fusion framework to improve contextual value alignment in large language models using multiple moral agents and iterative expansion-reduction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new framework called Multilayer Combinatorial Fusion for Contextual Value Alignment (MCF-CVA) has been proposed to enhance how large language models align with diverse human values. Unlike traditional single-agent methods, MCF-CVA employs multiple moral agents representing distinct values and combines their outputs through iterative expansion and reduction layers to better capture ethical pluralism and adapt to varying moral contexts. The framework uses a dual architecture involving Euclidean score space and Kemeny rank space to perform combinatorial fusion, mitigating conflicts and redundancies among agents. Empirical evaluations show that MCF-CVA outperforms single-agent baselines and previous multi-agent aggregation approaches on standard metrics, offering a more robust mechanism for trustworthy AI value alignment in language models.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Mendel Gödel Machine for recursive self-improving coding agents using comparative evolution and Mendelian inheritance principles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The Mendel Gödel Machine (MGM) is a new approach for self-improving coding agents that iteratively rewrite their own source code by leveraging comparative signals from multiple past attempts, inspired by Mendelian inheritance. MGM introduces reaction-norm mutation, which edits agents based on performance across multiple tasks, and cross-lineage hybridization, which uses trajectories from different agent lineages to enhance self-modification. Theoretical analysis and controlled simulations show that these strategies enable faster and more effective convergence compared to single-trajectory methods. Experiments on SWE-bench and Polyglot benchmarks demonstrate MGM's consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and generalizability across coding tasks.

entry.title: Researchers develop IntelliAudit, a multi-agent system using large language models to evaluate IT audit controls with evidence-grounded assessments and recommendations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have created IntelliAudit, a system that leverages large language models and multi-agent retrieval to assist IT auditors in evaluating compliance with security controls like ISO/IEC 27001. The system retrieves relevant organizational evidence, generates assessments based on that evidence, challenges adverse findings, and provides recommendations with supporting rationale and guidance. Evaluations with expert auditors and simulated organizations show that IntelliAudit supports control interpretation and audit preparation but requires human oversight to ensure accurate judgments and avoid overly permissive conclusions. IntelliAudit is designed as a decision-support tool rather than an autonomous certification system.

entry.title: Study proposes framework to assess and mitigate patient privacy risks in clinical foundation models amid gaps in HIPAA and GDPR [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A new study examines privacy risks from clinical foundation models trained on large-scale patient data, highlighting potential leakage of sensitive information that existing regulations like HIPAA and GDPR do not fully address. The authors propose a practical framework to evaluate privacy risks, demonstrate realistic scenarios where patient data could be exposed, and suggest combined technical and legal strategies to protect privacy while preserving model utility. Their analysis aims to provide context-aware risk assessments to support safe deployment of medical foundation models in decision support and public health applications.

entry.title: Researchers propose spectral fingerprinting method to trace large language model lineage using weight-space geometry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers investigate whether large language models (LLMs) have intrinsic fingerprints in their weight space that reveal their origin and lineage, without needing input data. They introduce a geometric fingerprinting framework analyzing spectral energy and subspace alignment of weight matrices to distinguish between independently trained models, same-series models, and shared-base models. Experiments on over 110 open-weight LLM pairs show that weight-space geometry provides a robust and interpretable signal for model provenance and governance. The study highlights a hierarchy of structural similarity in weight space, with spectral energy differentiating model families and subspace alignment enabling fine-grained discrimination among closely related models.

entry.title: Researchers identify and analyze the cross-lingual refusal circuit in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model, revealing language-invariant harm detection but late-stage refusal writing mechanisms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied safety alignment in sarvam, an Indic-multilingual mixture-of-experts reasoning model, finding that while harm detection is consistent across languages, the refusal to comply with harmful requests is generated late and through a distinct circuit. They located a specific mixture-of-experts writer circuit controlled by an attention opposer, with interventions on this circuit varying in cost and effectiveness. The circuit's structure and the gradient method used to expose it were also observed in a second unrelated MoE model, though the strength of the control lever depends on the model architecture. This work provides a cost-based map for implementing multilingual safety repairs in such models.

entry.title: Researchers propose PATH, an autoregressive tree hierarchy model for next-interval prediction on tabular data, achieving shorter prediction intervals with maintained coverage on 56 OpenML datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce PATH, a method that models interval prediction as a hierarchical process using binary trees to represent nested subintervals. PATH learns probability flows between intervals with an autoregressive decoder, enabling it to produce shorter prediction intervals while maintaining target coverage levels. The approach was evaluated against 24 baselines on PATHBench, a benchmark of 56 OpenML regression datasets, where it achieved the lowest mean normalized interval length of 0.1473 and mean coverage of 0.9144. This work demonstrates that hierarchical output modeling can effectively improve compact interval prediction on tabular data. The code for PATH is publicly available.

entry.title: Neurosymbolic Discovery of Algebraic Graph Constructions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There are several methods for searching for graphs with prescribed properties, such as SAT solvers and specialized generators. These methods return the result as raw data: an adjacency matrix or a string encoding. The raw data certifies that the graph exists, but it does not reveal any structural properties of the graph. We ask whether one can automatically discover a short algebraic description if only this raw data is provided. We look for a description such as a Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(\Gamma, S)$ or a lexicographic product $C_5[K_3]$. We address this question with a neurosymbolic approach. We propose an agent that runs on a general-purpose large language model with no fine-tuning or per-target training. The model interleaves reasoning with calls to the computer algebra system SageMath: it analyzes the target graph, proposes and tests candidate constructions, and revises them until the output matches the target. The agent communicates with SageMath through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which we release as a general-purpose bridge. Whether a construction matches the target is checked by a single exact isomorphism test, and therefore rests on the symbolic side and not on the model. We test the approach on a benchmark of 100 highly symmetric graphs, namely two-orbit graphs on up to 25 vertices; the benchmark was fixed in advance. Our agent could find verified algebraic constructions for all of them, without falling back to raw encodings. A strong template-enumeration baseline reaches only about $20\%$, and a catalog lookup could not identify any of these graphs. However, construction quality declines when symmetry is removed. As a concrete application, we identify the smallest known counterexample to the Bernhart-Kainen dispersability conjecture, a $16$-vertex graph that enumeration found as raw data. For this graph, our agent found an explicit algebraic construction.

entry.title: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Reward Shaping in Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse, delayed, and weakly informative rewards remain central obstacles to efficient reinforcement learning. Reward shaping addresses these limitations by supplementing the task reward with an auxiliary signal that can accelerate learning while, in the classical setting, the original objective remains the evaluation criterion. Established theory guarantees safety for fixed shaping signals: potential-based reward shaping preserves optimal policies when the auxiliary term is the discounted difference of a time-invariant potential. In contemporary reinforcement learning systems, however, both the learner and the information available for guidance evolve during training: value estimates improve, novelty diminishes, feedback shifts, and predictive models are refined. Adaptive reward mechanisms occur across exploration, Bayesian inference, human-in-the-loop learning, automated reward design, and foundation-model-based approaches. This study introduces a unified analytical framework for comparing dynamic reward shaping and neighbouring adaptive reward mechanisms. The proposed framework distinguishes parametric revision from state-dependent variation, separates additive shaping from reward replacement and reward-adjacent guidance, and organises existing methods along temporal, informational, and theoretical dimensions. Using this framework, twelve method families are comparatively analysed. The framework further highlights the conditions under which optimality guarantees survive contemporary deep reinforcement learning pipelines, replay buffers, bootstrapped critics, and reward normalisation, while exposing the unresolved relationship between adaptation rate and learner stability.

entry.title: Matching Supervision to the Student's Learning Capacity: A Unified Framework for On-Policy Self-Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves the reasoning abilities of LLMs by internalizing privileged context into model parameters through self-distillation. Two recent research lines promote vanilla OPSD by choosing which tokens to learn from and by controlling how much privileged information the teacher receives, respectively. However, we show that each line optimizes one variable while holding the other fixed, which leads to a suboptimal solution. We argue that the two variables are coupled through the student's learning capacity: the privileged information sets the per-token divergence the teacher prescribes, while token weighting selects which of these the student must absorb. We formalize the two lines of work into a unified optimization framework, which maximizes the aggregate teacher--student divergence, subject to a budget on the aggregate learning difficulty the student can absorb. Under this modelling, we propose Unified On-Policy Self-Distillation (USD), a lightweight online algorithm to solve the Lagrangian. USD reveals that a single dual variable governs both decisions: at one price for learning difficulty, it simultaneously sets the token-selection threshold and the direction of privileged-information adjustment, keeping supervision matched to the student's evolving capacity. Through extensive experiments, USD consistently demonstrates superior performance over OPSD and token- and PI-side baselines across various model scales on various reasoning benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/lauvlalala/USD.

entry.title: Harmful Content Is Not Enough: Continuation Framing Moderates In-Context Emergent Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) can induce emergent misalignment (EM), where narrow misaligned examples alter answers to unrelated questions. Existing prompts, however, conflate harmful-text exposure with an invitation to continue assistant behavior. We hold harmful answers fixed while varying their delivery as demonstrations, evidence, assistant history, or tool output. Across ten independently sampled contexts, demonstration framing raises broad EM by $30$--$32$ percentage points on a susceptible Gemini model; the gap survives domain exclusion, semantic clustering, unseen questions, and four prompt templates. Format and length-matched controls show that harmful content is necessary but insufficient. A role times continuation factorial further reveals model-dependent provenance effects: Gemini follows both assistant and tool histories, whereas Grok largely resists tool-framed continuation. Several other frontier and open-weight models show no gap. Blinded human audits confirm every main contrast and show that the model judge underestimates active-condition failures. Thus continuation framing is a strong, model-dependent moderator of ICL-EM, not a universal consequence of harmful context.

entry.title: LatticeMind: A Conflict-Aware Memory Primitive for Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems often fail not for lack of candidate answers, but because they have no persistent mechanism for deciding which incompatible claim should currently be trusted. Majority vote, debate, and judge-based selection choose an output without recording which claim wins, which is contested, or why a later update supersedes it. We present \term{LatticeMind}, a conflict-aware structured memory that handles contradiction at write time. It maintains explicit item status, applies cheap symbolic conflict checks, and invokes LLM reconciliation only for unresolved semantic cases. On a label-blind ConflictBank evaluation that removes source-name hints, LatticeMind reaches 0.97 accuracy versus 0.61 for the strongest aggregation baseline, with the gap significant at $p<10^{-6}$ by paired McNemar test. Ablations show that removing the checker or the reconciler costs 12 to 14 points. On four secondary planning benchmarks the picture is mixed: LatticeMind beats naive merge on three of four, but does not replace deliberation methods on tasks rewarding iterative search.

entry.title: Mitigating Over-Personalization in LLMs via Structured Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational assistants increasingly rely on persistent long-term memory to personalize responses across sessions. However, when stored user information is reintroduced into the model context, it can also influence responses in inappropriate or unrelated settings. We study two such failure modes in memory-augmented LLMs: cross-domain leakage, where memories from one life domain affect responses in another, and memory-induced sycophancy, where stored user beliefs make models more likely to agree with the user rather than respond truthfully. We apply a simple inference-time modification to how memories are presented to the model, without changing the model or the memory contents. Across seven models on PersistBench, we compare the commonly used all-in context format, where memories are injected as an unstructured list, with structured formats that partition memories by domain. This simple modification consistently reduces cross-domain leakage while preserving utility, with our strongest method reducing leakage by $8.8\%$ on average relative to the baseline.

entry.title: CAP: A Scalable Benchmark for Evaluating Cross-Site Browser Agents with Complex Actions and Perception [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that interact with the web through browsers. While recent progress has been driven by benchmarks that evaluate end-to-end task success, these evaluations largely overlook two fundamental sources of difficulty in real web browsing: complex actions over rich user interfaces and visual perception of dynamically rendered content, especially in workflows that span multiple websites. We introduce CAP, a scalable benchmark for evaluating browser agents on cross-site, human-like web tasks that require non-trivial UI interactions and visual understanding. Specifically, we adopt a decomposition-and-recomposition pipeline that first abstracts each website into a structured site card capturing user-facing functions, complex execution operations, and perceptual requirements, and then recomposes these components into realistic cross-site workflows. Each task is therefore grounded in multiple specific operations on each website, enabling fine-grained diagnosis. Built on this framework, we construct 420 tasks across 108 real-world websites and 24 domains under careful quality control. Experiments on state-of-the-art browser agents using our verifiable agent-as-a-judge evaluation framework show low success rates and reveal that perception-heavy interactions remain a major bottleneck, exposing substantial gaps between current agents and real-world web browsing demands.

entry.title: LLM within MCP Matters: Measuring Inefficient Resource Utilization Driven by LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how servers expose data and tools to Large Language Models (LLMs). A common server design embeds frequently used reference data, such as identifier lookup tables, directly in the server instructions: the system-prompt text a server hands to the host application. When a query concerns an entry of the embedded table, the model can act on it immediately instead of re-discovering the same information through a search tool. We test whether client LLMs actually consume such instruction-embedded data, reporting a 54,000-trial study across 24 LLMs (9 Claude, 6 Gemini, 9 GPT) on a production legal-information MCP server. A diagnostic condition that removes the competing search tool shows that failures are dominated by behavioral preference rather than missing capability. With search unavailable, 23 of 24 models read the embedded data reliably (hit ratio at least 98%); with a search tool merely present, 9 models drop below 15%. A 2^3 factorial analysis of three instruction-level interventions reveals strong interaction effects: combining all three restores at least 86% for 20 of 24 models, but individual interventions can backfire for specific model families. Per-server prompt engineering is therefore a workaround rather than a fix; we argue that MCP host applications should provide an explicit mechanism that places server instructions ahead of tool selection in the client LLM's deliberation.

entry.title: MathShikkha: A Controlled Study of Answer-Only and Chain-of-Thought Supervision for Bangla Mathematical Reasoning in Small Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical reasoning remains challenging in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We study whether teacher-generated Bangla Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision provides benefits beyond ordinary supervised fine-tuning. We construct \textsc{MathShikkha}, a Bangla mathematical reasoning dataset with GPT-5.4-generated rationales, and fine-tune four 4B--7B student models under a matched protocol in which answer-only and CoT conditions share data splits, response-only loss masking, decoding, and scoring, differing only in the training target. In-domain, CoT provides no significant improvement over answer-only fine-tuning for three stronger backbones (paired bootstrap 95\% CIs include zero; exact McNemar $p \geq 0.17$), despite generating 15--52$\times$ more tokens, but significantly improves the weaker 4B model by 18.56 points ($p < 0.0001$). On the larger, contamination-audited BanglaMATH benchmark, this pattern reverses: CoT significantly outperforms answer-only supervision for all four models by 20.1--28.1 points (all $p < 0.0001$). Answer-only fine-tuning also reduces out-of-domain accuracy below the base model for three models, whereas CoT preserves or improves it for all four. A human study with two co-author annotators, external-expert adjudication, and Cohen's $\kappa = 0.76$--$1.00$ finds no significant CoT improvement over the base model on reasoning-content criteria; instead, its measurable effect is target-language adherence and producing inspectable reasoning. Overall, rationale supervision's value depends on backbone capability and distribution shift: in this setting, its main benefits are Bangla adherence, auditable reasoning, and out-of-domain robustness rather than improved in-domain reasoning validity.

entry.title: Understanding Calibration and Truncation Error Propagation in Training-Free Low-Rank Compression for LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training-free low-rank compression frameworks have been gaining prominence for LLM compression given their effectiveness in reducing model parameter count while maintaining task-level accuracy. However, existing SOTA frameworks share two key limitations: (1) residual errors in calibration data activations accumulate across layers during compression, causing misalignment between representations simulated at compression time and those experienced at inference; (2) the assumption that layer importance distribution is preserved post-compression does not hold. Together, these two effects introduce misalignment in the compression process in relation to the deployed model. We study these effects and propose a simple, training-free methodology compatible with existing frameworks to mitigate them, comprising: (1) Layer-by-Layer Compression with Calibration Correction; (2) Iterative Compression with Rank Allocation Correction. Implemented atop an existing SOTA decomposition framework, and evaluated on Llama and Qwen3 models across various benchmarks and compression rates, our approach demonstrates up to ~1-2.5 accuracy point improvements over per-weight and joint decomposition baselines on zero-shot tasks.

entry.title: Can Open-Weight Models Compete on Financial Text Comprehension? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models from Chinese AI labs caught up on benchmarks relative to proprietary frontier models in recent months. Yet their reliability on real-world financial tasks remains largely untested. We updated the Financial Touchstone benchmark, which now has 2,967 question context-answer triplets across 495 international annual reports. We also apply a new set of models on the benchmark, expanding coverage from eleven to twenty models across ten providers, including recent open-weight models such as GLM 4.7, GLM 5, Kimi K2.6, and DeepSeek V3.2, as well as Alibaba's proprietary flagship Qwen3-Max. Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 achieves the highest accuracy (88.4%), while Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro maintains the lowest hallucination rate (0.08%). Notably, the open-weight Kimi K2.6 ranks third in accuracy, and the non-reasoning models GLM 5 and Mistral 3 rank fourth and fifth, challenging the assumption that reasoning architectures or proprietary weights are a prerequisite for strong financial comprehension. Information retrieval remains the primary bottleneck, accounting for 48.9% of all failures. We also document a new finding: geopolitical content filters in Chinese models refuse legitimate financial questions (0.08% of attempts), sometimes without clear reason, and the refusal behavior depends on the access route as much as on the model. The complete dataset and evaluation framework are publicly available.

entry.title: Automated Generation of Complexity-Validated Decision Scenarios Using Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive decision-making research depends on diverse scenarios with carefully controlled complexity, yet manual production is slow, inconsistent, and biased. We developed an automated pipeline that uses LLms to generate structured decision scenarios and validates their complexity through a composite framework rooted in established task-complexity theory. We evaluated 4,238 scenarios across multiple domains and complexity tiers. Measurement validation met rigorous psychometric standards. Agreement among five independent model families was nearly perfect, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.997 and a kappa of 0.971. Known-groups validity demonstrated large separation between tiers, with an eta-squared of 0.587 and all pairwise comparisons significant at p less than .001. Factor analysis revealed a dominant complexity construct, with loadings between 0.87 and 0.96 across three frameworks, while interactivity formed a weaker secondary dimension at 0.34. Discriminant validity was limited by a strong relationship between complexity and text length that persisted after controlling for tier, yielding a partial correlation of 0.86. This constrains construct purity but does not undermine the instrument's tier-grading function. Model analyses showed a negative association between throughput and schema pass rate (r = -0.967, p = .007, n = 5), suggesting a speed-quality trade-off, though largely driven by one high-throughput model. Llama 4 Maverick generated scenarios fastest at 134 per minute versus 25 for DeepSeek Chat V3.2, but underproduced complex-tier scenarios, whereas DeepSeek Chat V3.2 balanced domain coverage with high schema compliance. The system demonstrated strong psychometric properties, enabling reliable classification into Simple, Moderate, and Complex tiers and providing the measurement infrastructure needed for downstream cognitive assessment of AI systems

entry.title: Theory-Guided Deception Detection: A RAG-Based Artificial Intelligence Exploration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The current work developed seven Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models based on leading deception theories and compared how deception judgments were made relative to baseline models. Across 700 statements drawn from five published deception datasets, four large language models (gpt-4o, claude-sonnet-4-6, ollama/llama3, deepseek-v4-flash), and two run-types (RAG vs. baseline), a total of 39,200 deception judgments were rendered. Detection accuracies were consistent with typical human accuracies and not statistically different across RAG (54.5%) and baseline models (54.6%). RAG-based models (57.0%) were less truth-biased than baseline models (59.7%), but the effect size was quite small. Theoretical perspective mattered little for accuracy yet mattered substantially for response bias, which ranged from highly lie-biased (the verifiability approach, 32.2%) to highly truth-biased (truth-default theory, 88.1%). Content effects and model effects further moderated the results. Theory-guided AI judgments are unreliable with current parameters, yet they might show promise with additional datasets, model testing, and theory-to-data matching.

entry.title: Decoding Phenotypes: A Framework for Fusing Genomic Language Models and Neuroimaging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.08926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuroimaging and genetic testing are two important clinical references for nervous system diseases, offering complementary diagnostic information. However, integrating genomic and neuroimaging data for precise disease diagnosis is challenging due to cross-modality heterogeneity. Existing imaging-genetics approaches mainly encode genetic information as hard-coded labels, which lose the local sequence context around disease-associated variants. To address this limitation, we propose GeneFuse, a multimodal learning framework that aligns genetic representations from pre-trained Genomic Language Models (GLMs) with features extracted from images. GeneFuse integrates two components: (1) Genotype-Conditioned Feature Modulation (GCFM), a FiLM-inspired module that uses genomic embeddings to modulate image feature maps; and (2) Uncertainty-aware Genomic Residual Fusion (U-GRF), a fusion strategy that uses imaging-derived predictive uncertainty to gate the contribution of genotypic features. We evaluate GeneFuse on early cognitive decline identification (NC vs. MCI) and dementia screening (NC vs. AD). In the APOE-centered setting, GeneFuse achieves AUROCs of 0.77 and 0.83, outperforming existing imaging-genetics fusion methods. These results indicate that GLM-derived genomic embeddings provide additional information to imaging.

entry.title: PolicyKG: An Agentic LLM Pipeline for Translating Institutional Policies into SHACL Knowledge Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.09028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Institutional policies stay in natural language while the systems that check compliance demand machine-readable constraints. Bridging that gap is still done by hand. PolicyKG closes the loop. It is an LLM pipeline that reads a policy PDF, classifies each sentence as an obligation, permission, or prohibition, lifts the label into first-order deontic logic, and emits SHACL constraints. Four stages run on a LangGraph state machine with per-stage validators. The piece that matters most is the Corpus Adapter: a YAML vocabulary registry that grounds LLM predicates in a target ontology. Retargeting to a new domain means swapping the registry, not retraining a model. On the Asian Institute of Technology Policies and Procedures corpus (1,663 sentences, 443 rules), PolicyKG reaches 86.9% deontic classification accuracy (Cohen's kappa = .709). Three annotators independently re-label a 50-item sample and agree at Fleiss' kappa = .844. SHACL shape correctness on a 69-shape subset is F1 = .866. The FOL path handles 79.2% of rules; the rest go through a direct NL-to-SHACL fallback. We audited every one of the 443 rules for second- or higher-order constructs. An automated regex checklist flagged none, and a first-author pass on the 92 FOL-fallback cases confirmed the same. The exact upper 95% Clopper-Pearson bound on the true HOL rate is 0.67%. This is an audit finding for one corpus, not a proof of FOL sufficiency for institutional policy. Swapping the AIT registry for a GDPR registry raises exact property alignment from 1/15 to 11/15 (Fisher's exact p < .001; Cohen's h = 1.53). On the LexDeMod lease-contract benchmark (N = 200), Macro F1 drops to .370 because lease English uses "shall be entitled" for permission -- exactly the vocabulary mismatch registry swap is meant to fix. Repeated runs produce hash-identical SHACL outputs.

entry.title: A Multi-Scale Temporal Framework with Dynamic Fusion for EEG-Based Emotion Recognition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.09088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed emotions represent a clinically relevant but still underexplored target for automatic emotion recognition. EEG provides millisecond-level access to neural activity, yet most EEG pipelines analyze the signal through a single temporal window, thereby fixing the temporal structure available to the model. This study introduces a multi-scale temporal framework for EEG-based emotion recognition. The EEG waveform is decomposed into windows of one or several durations, processed by a shared attention-based encoder, and integrated through a dynamic fusion module that assigns sample-specific weights across temporal scales. The framework is evaluated under a subject-independent protocol in binary and three-class settings, with the three-class task including the mixed affective category. The best results are 65.22% for the two-class task and 45.43% for the three-class task. Both are obtained with three-scale dynamic-fusion configurations and remain substantially above the full-signal baseline. The best-performing temporal scales differ between the two tasks. Dynamic fusion outperforms concatenation in the highest-scoring two-class configuration and slightly exceeds it in the highest-scoring three-class configuration, although these multi-scale settings require substantially more computation than the full-signal baseline.

entry.title: TRACE: TRajectory Attribution for Automated Context Engineering [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.09153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Production AI agents fail when their context sources -- system prompts, knowledge bases, tool descriptions, and procedural skills -- contain errors or gaps. Current maintenance relies on manual log review and ad-hoc debugging, creating a scalability bottleneck as interaction volume grows. We present TRACE (TRajectory Attribution for Automated Context Engineering), an automated feedback loop that mines historical agent trajectories to diagnose and remediate context failures. Our key insight is that trajectories are rich with implicit dissatisfaction signals -- user corrections, rephrasing, abandonment cues -- that reveal precisely where context sources failed, without explicit feedback collection. Unlike model fine-tuning, TRACE operates on the context layer, enabling rapid iteration without retraining.
